reading.rtitle: Eleven Rooms, One Voice -- a retrospective in Houston
paras: The artist whose retrospective opened last week in Houston has never shown in Brazil, which is the first thing worth saying about an exhibition that took eleven years to assemble. Thirty-one works, none of them famous, and a hang so restrained that the first room holds only four paintings.

The early canvases are figurative and loud. Faces, doorways, a kitchen table, and a palette so bright that the wall behind them seems to retreat. Then, in the room where the nineties begin, everything goes quiet. The colors turn muted, the brushwork loosens, and the paintings stop announcing themselves.

The centre of the show is a small canvas called Evening, Interior, which the artist painted in 1998, the year she returned to figurative work after a decade of pure color. Stand close enough and the texture gives the game away: the surface is layered, and at least three earlier compositions sit underneath the one you are looking at. It is the most evocative object in the building, and it is the size of a book.

There is one bold decision, and it is the curator's. The largest painting, the one that everybody photographs, has been hung last instead of first, at the end of a corridor where it can be seen only from thirty metres away. The effect is deliberate and slightly cruel: by the time you reach it, you have learned to prefer the quiet ones. This is an understated show about an artist who spent thirty years getting quieter, and it is the best thing in Texas this season.

gist.prompt: What is this review mainly saying?
choices: That the exhibition is too small and should have included more famous works
That the show follows an artist who grew quieter, and that the quiet works are the best of it
That the museum should hang the largest painting at the entrance instead

listenings.text: This is the tour I give when someone has twenty minutes. We start here, in the room with only four paintings on the wall, and people always ask why. The answer is that these works are quiet, and if I fill the wall you will walk past them. The restraint is deliberate. Eleven works in a room that could hold thirty. Now, the small canvas in the centre, Evening, Interior. Please stand closer than feels polite, because the texture is the argument. The surface is layered, and there are at least three earlier paintings underneath the one you can see. Nineteen ninety-eight is the year everything changes for her. She comes back to figurative work after a decade of pure color, and at the same moment the palette goes muted, grey and sand and one faded blue that appears only in the chair. And finally, the enormous one at the end of the corridor, the one everybody photographs. It is the boldest thing she ever painted, and it is not the best. The best is the small one you have just walked away from, and I hang the big one last so that you find that out for yourself.

People are not afraid of art. People are afraid of being caught saying something naive in front of somebody who knows more than they do, which is a completely different fear and a much easier one to solve. My formula has two parts, and I have never needed a third. Part one: name one thing you can actually see. The brushwork is loose. The palette is muted. The texture is thick at the window and flat in the corners. Nobody can argue with what is in front of both of you. Part two: say what it does to you. It makes the room feel like early evening. It reminds me of my grandmother's kitchen. That is your opinion, and it is unarguable too, because it is yours. What holds the two halves together is a relative clause. The canvas which hangs alone is the one I keep going back to. The artist whose palette went quiet after ninety-eight is the one I would collect. The evidence travels inside the sentence, so the judgement never arrives naked. And one last thing. The only sentence that really disqualifies you in a gallery is I do not know much about art. In thirty years nobody has ever asked me for my credentials in front of a painting.

extra_audio.text: First, you look for longer than feels comfortable, and you name one thing you can actually see: the brushwork, the texture, the palette. Then, you say what the work does to you, because that half of the opinion is yours and nobody can argue with it. After that, you attach the reason to the judgement with a relative clause, so the evidence travels inside the sentence instead of arriving later. Next, you place the work in the artist's story: what changed, and when, and whether this canvas comes before or after that change. Finally, you give your verdict in one sentence, and you say whether you would live with the work or only visit it.
